title: Large language model assistance for report-based carotid plaque AHA classification: a multi-reader study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether large language model assistance improves radiologists' agreement with a text-based reference standard in inferring the modified American Heart Association carotid plaque classification from free-text MRI reports, and whether a lightweight model can perform well under criteria-guided prompting. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 433 patients from three institutions. In a report-based reader study, four radiologists classified MRI reports with and without large language model assistance. In standalone evaluation, a rule-based baseline and 10 models were compared under naive and criteria-guided prompting. The reference standard was expert consensus based on the report text. Results Among 433 patients (mean age, 65.9 years ± 13.4; 248 males), AI assistance improved six-class agreement with the text-based reference standard. At the vessel level, junior radiologists improved from 61.75% to 83.12% (Qwen3-8B) and 87.75% (DeepSeek-R1); senior radiologists from 77.00% to 87.50% and 92.25%, respectively (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001). Patient-level agreement increased from 41.0% to 78.8% (junior) and from 59.8% to 87.8% (senior) with DeepSeek-R1. Agreement increased (quadratic-weighted κ: 0.231 without AI vs 0.775 with DeepSeek-R1). In standalone evaluation, criteria-guided prompting improved Qwen3-8B agreement from 38.91% to 81.52% (95% CI: 78.87-84.06%), remaining 5.89 percentage points below DeepSeek-R1 (87.41%; 95% CI: 85.10-89.61%). Conclusion In this report-based classification setting, large language model assistance improved radiologists' agreement with the text-based reference standard, with larger gains in junior radiologists. When prompts explicitly encoded AHA criteria, an 8B local candidate model performed well, supporting its potential use as a standardization aid for text-based workflows. Key points Question Report-based modified AHA classification of carotid plaques is experience-dependent and difficult to standardize, as mapping multi-sequence imaging findings to classification conclusions imposes substantial cognitive load. Findings Large language model assistance improved agreement with a text-based reference standard and raised inter-reader consistency (weighted κ 0.231-0.775), narrowing the junior-senior gap. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

title: Multimodal imaging features of nuclear protein in testis carcinoma of the submandibular gland: a case report.
abstract: Rationale NUT carcinoma (NC) is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy defined by rearrangements of the NUTM1gene. Primary NC of the submandibular gland is exceptionally rare, with nonspecific imaging features that often lead to misdiagnosis as common salivary gland tumors and delayed treatment. Patient concerns A 32-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the left submandibular region that rapidly enlarged from 2 cm to approximately 4 cm within 1 month, accompanied by the development of ipsilateral pharyngeal and periauricular pain. Diagnoses Preoperative multimodal imaging-computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-revealed an ill-defined, invasive mass with heterogeneous enhancement and intense metabolic activity (SUVmax 18.4). The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis, which demonstrated diffuse nuclear positivity for NUT protein. Interventions The patient underwent radical surgical resection (left neck dissection), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Outcomes No evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease was observed on follow-up imaging at 9 months postoperatively. Lessons This case underscores that although the imaging features of submandibular gland NC are not pathognomonic, the combination of a rapidly growing invasive mass, heterogeneous enhancement, and marked hypermetabolism should raise clinical suspicion. Prompt biopsy with NUT immunohistochemical testing is essential for definitive diagnosis and early intervention, which is critical given the tumor's highly aggressive nature.

Rationale

NUT carcinoma (NC) is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy defined by rearrangements of the NUTM1gene. Primary NC of the submandibular gland is exceptionally rare, with nonspecific imaging features that often lead to misdiagnosis as common salivary gland tumors and delayed treatment.

Patient concerns

A 32-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the left submandibular region that rapidly enlarged from 2 cm to approximately 4 cm within 1 month, accompanied by the development of ipsilateral pharyngeal and periauricular pain.

Preoperative multimodal imaging-computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-revealed an ill-defined, invasive mass with heterogeneous enhancement and intense metabolic activity (SUVmax 18.4). The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis, which demonstrated diffuse nuclear positivity for NUT protein.

The patient underwent radical surgical resection (left neck dissection), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Outcomes

No evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease was observed on follow-up imaging at 9 months postoperatively.

Lessons

This case underscores that although the imaging features of submandibular gland NC are not pathognomonic, the combination of a rapidly growing invasive mass, heterogeneous enhancement, and marked hypermetabolism should raise clinical suspicion. Prompt biopsy with NUT immunohistochemical testing is essential for definitive diagnosis and early intervention, which is critical given the tumor's highly aggressive nature.

title: Fully automated diaphragm segmentation on routine 2D-cine and 3D thoracic MRI: multireader validation.
abstract: Objective The diaphragm is central to respiratory mechanics and may be impaired in various diseases. Parametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment is limited by time-consuming manual segmentation. We developed and validated fully automated diaphragm segmentation on two-dimensional (2D)-cine and three-dimensional (3D) thoracic MRI. Materials and methods In this single-center study, eligible adults without known diaphragmatic disorders underwent 2D-cine MRI, 3D MRI, or both. Two U-Net models (2D/3D) were trained using expert manual contours as ground truth. Performance was evaluated with normalized surface Dice (NSD) with 3-voxel tolerance and average surface distance (ASSD). In the main cohort, five blinded radiologists rated segmentation usability and image quality. An additional separate pathology cohort was assessed by two blinded readers using the same scale. Results Overall, 59 individuals contributed 70 MRI acquisitions: 29 women, 30 men; aged 49.3 ± 18.8 years (mean ± standard deviation). Inference required 5 s (2D) and 30 s (3D) versus 10 min and 4.5 h for manual annotation. Segmentation accuracy was high: NSD 0.95 ± 0.08 (2D) and 0.92 ± 0.06 (3D), with ASSD 1.97 ± 2.29 mm (2D) and 1.88 ± 1.97 mm (3D). In the main cohort, segmentations were rated clinically usable in 87.5% (2D) and 100% (3D). Mean image-quality scores were 4.0/5 (2D) and 4.2/5 (3D) and correlated with segmentation quality. In the pathology cohort (n = 5), segmentation usability for 2D images was 75% for reader 1 and 70% for reader 2 for 2D images and 80% for both readers for 3D volumes. Conclusion Automated diaphragm segmentation on 2D-cine and 3D MRI is feasible, accurate, and time-efficient, supporting scalable, standardized diaphragm analysis as a basis for deriving diaphragm biomarkers. Key points Question Can fully automated diaphragm segmentation make routine 2D-cine and 3D thoracic MRI analysis clinically feasible by replacing time-consuming manual delineation? Findings Automated segmentation achieved normalized surface Dice above 0.9, radiologist acceptability in 87.5-100% of cases, and inference times below 30 s Relevance statement Automated diaphragm segmentation on routine 2D-cine and 3D static MRI yields accurate, radiologist-acceptable segmentations with normalized surface Dice exceeding 0.9 and mean surface deviations below 2 mm. This approach may support standardized diaphragm assessment for objective quantification in thoracic and neuromuscular imaging pending larger multicenter validation.

title: Diagnostic challenges of masked arginine vasopressin deficiency in neurosarcoidosis complicated by sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor use.
abstract: A wide variety of endocrine disorders caused by sarcoidosis have been reported to date. We report the case of an 82-year-old male patient who presented with hypercalcemia and anterior pituitary hormone deficiency at the time of his sarcoidosis diagnosis and was subsequently diagnosed with arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) 6 months after the initiation of glucocorticoid therapy. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an enlarged pituitary gland, thickened pituitary stalk, and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot, raising the suspicion of hypothalamic-pituitary sarcoidosis. Despite improvement in hypercalcemia, anterior pituitary function, and pituitary enlargement and stalk thickening with glucocorticoid therapy, subjective symptoms of dry mouth and polyuria gradually became apparent several months after the start of treatment. While the characteristic hypotonic polyuria of AVP-D was not prominent, we surmised that these typical clinical features were masked by adrenal insufficiency, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and concurrent use of a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor for type 2 diabetes. This case highlights the fact that the typical presentation of AVP-D can be masked by concurrent SGLT2 inhibitor use and CKD, emphasizing careful assessment of water balance in such patients.

title: White Matter Functional Disconnection Predicts Long-Term Disability and Early Mortality in Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Background and objectives Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) has the highest short-term mortality among stroke subtypes, and progress in treatment has been hindered by the limited accuracy of current prognostic tools. We investigated whether white matter functional disconnection severity, estimated using a normative lesion network mapping framework integrating direct electrical stimulation and resting-state functional MRI data from previously published independent Data sets, improves prediction of 6-month functional outcome measured with the modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Methods We analyzed 97 patients with spontaneous ICH. Ordinal logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between domain-specific disconnection severity and 6-month mRS, and to compare traditional functional outcome in patients with primary intracerebral hemorrhage and ICH scores with connectivity-enriched models incorporating disconnection measures. Results White matter functional disconnectivity was significantly associated with 6-month functional outcome (mRS; P < .001; Nagelkerke's R2 = 0.507). Integrating disconnection severity into the functional outcome in patients with primary intracerebral hemorrhage and ICH scores improved predictive performance in both cases (Nagelkerke's R2 = 0.615 vs 0.389 and 0.651 vs 0.434, respectively), with the connectivity-enriched ICH score achieving the strongest overall fit across all models tested. Exploratory analyses showed associations between domain-specific disconnection severity, residual functional deficits, and early mortality. Conclusion Assessment of white matter functional disconnection severity seems to be a promising approach for predicting long-term disability after ICH, although prospective validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required before clinical implementation. The findings suggest that different brain networks exhibit variable vulnerability to injury and differential potential for functional recovery.

title: Large Carinal Chondrosarcoma: Resection of the Main Carina, Distal Trachea, and Orifices of the Mainstem Bronchi and Construction of a New Carina.
abstract: BACKGROUND Chondrosarcoma of the trachea is an extremely rare malignancy, and tumors located at the main carina are even rarer. Carinal resection and subsequent reconstruction of a new carina constitute a demanding surgical procedure that requires extensive expertise and close collaboration between the anesthetic and surgical teams. In this case report, we aim to highlight the rarity of chondrosarcoma of the main carina and emphasize the critical role of surgical intervention despite the complexity of the procedure. Furthermore, we aim to share our clinical experience and contribute an additional case to the limited literature. CASE REPORT A 23-year-old man presented with dyspnea, fatigue, and cough. Chest computed tomography showed a lobulated soft-tissue mass anterior to the distal trachea and main carina. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed widening of the main carina, clinically significant stenosis of the mainstem bronchi, and mucosal infiltration. Biopsy specimens obtained via mediastinoscopy demonstrated well-differentiated carinal chondrosarcoma. Through a right posterolateral thoracotomy, the distal trachea, main carina, and orifices of the mainstem bronchi were resected. A new carina was constructed and anastomosed to the distal trachea. Gross examination of the surgical specimen showed a well-circumscribed mass with a lobulated external surface measuring 7×6.5×5 cm. The patient remains well 17 years after tumor resection, without signs of recurrence. CONCLUSIONS Chondrosarcoma involving the distal trachea and main carina is an extremely rare tumor. Given the limited efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, surgical resection with reconstruction of a new carina is the primary treatment.

title: Histopathologic spectrum of focal liver lesions diagnosed by ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy and predictors of hepatocellular carcinoma: A single-center experience from Sub-Saharan Africa.
abstract: Background Focal liver lesions (FLLs) encompass a wide spectrum of benign and malignant pathologies, and accurate diagnosis is essential for appropriate management. Although advances in imaging have improved lesion characterization, histopathologic assessment remains the diagnostic gold standard for indeterminate lesions. Data on the histopathologic spectrum and diagnostic utility of ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy (US-PLB) in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) are limited. This study aimed to characterize the histopathologic findings of US-PLB performed for FLLs at a tertiary referral center in SSA and to identify factors associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent US-PLB for FLL between January 2021 and December 2024 at Adera Medical and Surgical Center. Patients with indeterminate pathology results, incomplete records, biopsies performed for diffuse liver disease, or lesions classified as LI-RADS 1, 2, or 5 were excluded. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, imaging, histopathologic, and outcome data were extracted from medical records. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics and histopathologic diagnoses. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with HCC. Results A total of 119 were included in the final analysis. The median age was 56 years (IQR 45-65), and 59.7% were male. The median focal liver lesion size was 8.20 cm (IQR: 5.1-11.0 cm), with 38.7% presenting as multifocal lesions. No major biopsy-related complications were reported. HCC was the most common histopathologic diagnosis, accounting for 42.9% of cases, followed by secondary metastatic tumors (15.9%) and regenerative nodules (15.9%). Other diagnoses included chronic hepatitis (8.4%), cholangiocarcinoma (5.9%), and hepatic abscess (3.4%). Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections were present in 14.3% and 12.4% of patients, respectively. On multivariate analysis, HBV infection (AOR 7.85, 95% CI 1.45-42.60; p = 0.017), HCV infection (AOR 9.03, 95% CI 1.41-57.76; p = 0.020), Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score (AOR 1.45, 95% CI: 1.05-2.34: p < 0.01), and larger tumor size (AOR 1.27, 95% CI 1.11-1.46; p < 0.01) were significantly associated with HCC. Conclusion Ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated a favorable safety profile for the evaluation of FLL. HCC was the predominant histopathologic diagnosis, reflecting the substantial burden of primary liver cancer in this setting. Chronic viral hepatitis and larger tumor size were significantly associated with HCC. These findings support the continued role of US-PLB in the diagnostic evaluation of indeterminate focal liver lesions and underscores the importance of viral hepatitis prevention, surveillance, and early detection strategies in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Pediatric prolactinoma-associated pituitary apoplexy presenting with acute visual loss: a case report, literature review, and management strategy.
abstract: Objectives Hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy (PA) in children is exceedingly rare, with approximately 32 cases reported since 1980. Current guidelines recommend cabergoline as first-line therapy; however, acute complete visual loss mandates emergency surgical decompression. No guideline defines the optimal extent of resection, despite gross total resection carrying a 48-54 % risk of panhypopituitarism. Case presentation An 11-year-old prepubertal girl presented with a 2-day history of complete right-eye visual loss. Serum prolactin was 987 μg/L, and MRI demonstrated a hemorrhagic sellar-suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Emergency endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery was performed with an intentionally limited strategy - hematoma evacuation, optic decompression, and partial debulking - deliberately avoiding aggressive capsular dissection. Histopathology confirmed prolactinoma. Vision was fully restored immediately after extubation, with near-complete visual field recovery on postoperative day 5 (VFI 98 %). Adrenocortical function was preserved. Central hypothyroidism developed, and levothyroxine was initiated. Cabergoline (0.25 mg/week) was started on postoperative day 5, achieving a 93.7 % prolactin reduction by day 20 (987 → 61.9 μg/L). Conclusions In pediatric prolactinoma-associated PA requiring emergency surgery, a decompression-first strategy prioritizing visual rescue and tissue diagnosis over gross total resection may reduce the risk of panhypopituitarism, with residual tumor subsequently managed with cabergoline. The rapid biochemical response documented here supports this approach, though multicenter prospective evaluation is required.

title: Pulsatile Tinnitus: A Multimodality Imaging Review of Etiology and Diagnostic Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Pulsatile tinnitus is a rhythmic, pulse-synchronous auditory perception that is frequently associated with an underlying vascular or structural abnormality. While tinnitus affects approximately 10–20% of adults, pulsatile tinnitus is relatively uncommon but clinically significant, with an identifiable and potentially treatable cause detected in over 70% of patients and in up to 90% in dedicated imaging cohorts. The etiologic spectrum is broad and includes vascular, structural, systemic, benign, and malignant conditions, some of which may result in serious morbidity if unrecognized. Imaging is central to diagnosis and management, with evaluation commonly performed using high-resolution temporal bone CT, CT angiography and venography, MRI with angiographic and venographic techniques, and digital subtraction angiography in selected cases. This pictorial review integrates multimodality imaging with representative case examples to provide a structured, physiology-based diagnostic approach. By emphasizing key imaging patterns across major etiologic categories, this review aims to enhance diagnostic confidence, streamline imaging workup, and facilitate recognition of actionable causes, thereby supporting timely intervention and improved patient outcomes.

title: Impact of coronary artery calcification detection on cardiovascular care trajectories in patients undergoing lung cancer screening: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Importance: Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is commonly identified on low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) performed for lung cancer screening (LCS) and is associated with increased cardiovascular (CV) risk. Although guidelines increasingly recommend reporting and incorporating CAC into CV risk stratification, whether its detection translates into downstream CV preventive care remains unclear. Objective: To systematically evaluate reporting practices and downstream clinical management following CAC detection during LDCT LCS. Evidence Review: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science Core Collection from inception to September 23, 2026, and searched grey literature through September 20, 2026. We included original studies of adults undergoing LDCT within established or pilot LCS programs if they evaluated downstream management following CAC detection or reporting. Reviewers independently extracted data in duplicate on CAC assessment, reporting, communication, preventive pharmacotherapy, referrals, investigations, and clinical outcomes. We assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, we synthesized findings narratively. Findings: We included twelve studies published between 2020 and 2026 from the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and France. Visual assessment was the predominant method for CAC identification, although reporting and communication practices varied substantially. Statin initiation (N=7) ranged from 3% to 38%, cardiology referral (N=3) from 6.9% to 44%, and cardiac stress testing (N=2) from 12.5% to 21.6%. Structured CV follow-up pathways were evaluated in five studies. Three studies found greater a CAC severity or a more explicit reporting was associated with increased statin initiation. Study quality was moderate overall, with NOS scores ranging from four to eight of nine; common limitations included absence of comparator groups and limited adjustment for confounding. Conclusions and Relevance: CAC detected during LCS was followed by variable downstream CV preventive care, and reporting alone does not consistently translate into clinical action. Greater CAC severity and more explicit reporting were associated with increased clinical action in some studies, but reporting alone did not consistently translate into preventive management. Comparative studies are needed to determine whether structured communication and follow-up pathways improve cardiovascular care and clinical outcomes.

title: Striatal tissue iron in depressed and healthy individuals and the effect of buproprion
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Dopaminergic dysfunction in the striatum is thought to play a central role in anhedonia in major depressive disorder (MDD). Normalised T2*-weighted (nT2*w) imaging provides a widely available MRI-derived proxy of striatal tissue iron, an indirect marker of dopaminergic function, but its relationship with reward processing and anhedonia in MDD has not been established. In this secondary analysis, we examined whether striatal nT2*w distinguishes individuals with MDD from healthy controls, is associated with reward learning and clinical symptoms, including anhedonia and depression, and is sensitive to treatment with the dopaminergic antidepressant bupropion Methods Depressed (n = 40) and healthy participants (n = 41) underwent clinical assessment, functional MRI, and a probabilistic instrumental learning task (PILT) at baseline, with follow-up assessments after 2 and 6 weeks. Participants with MDD received open-label bupropion treatment throughout the 6-week study. The primary outcome was MRI-derived striatal tissue iron, quantified using nT2*w signal extracted from resting-state fMRI within the whole striatum, caudate, putamen, and nucleus accumbens. Associations between nT2*w, diagnostic group, reward learning, clinical symptoms, and treatment response were examined. Results At baseline, depressed participants compared to healthy controls showed significantly higher striatal and caudate nT2*w values, indicative of lower tissue iron. The marker demonstrated excellent 2-week test-retest reliability in healthy participants. Striatal nT2*w was not associated with reward learning, anhedonia, or depression severity at baseline, and did not change following 2 weeks of bupropion treatment or predict clinical response after 6 weeks. Across groups, females demonstrated higher nT2*w values (lower tissue iron) than males in the striatum, caudate, and putamen. Discussion Striatal nT2*w represents a promising, robust and widely accessible neuroimaging marker of depression, reliably distinguishing depressed individuals from healthy controls while demonstrating excellent test–retest reliability. Larger longitudinal studies are now needed to establish its clinical utility and determine whether it can detect changes in reward processing and treatment response across the course of illness.

title: Improving Postpolypectomy Surveillance Decisions Using an Automated Analysis of Colonoscopy and Histopathology Reports: 2-Center Validation Study.
abstract: Background Postpolypectomy surveillance intervals derived from colonoscopy findings and histopathology should be guideline-based, yet these are frequently not adhered to, contributing to under- and oversurveillance. This motivates a more structured and automated approach to improve adherence. Objective We developed and evaluated an automated, implementable, guideline-aligned decision support tool that extracts colorectal polyp features from free-text colonoscopy and histopathology reports and produces auditable surveillance recommendations. Methods We extracted paired colonoscopy and histopathology reports from a National Health Service (NHS) trust and designed a 4-stage prompting pipeline using open-weight large language models to separate multispecimen histopathology reports into individual containers ("pots"), align endoscopic findings with specimens, and normalize each pot into a structured schema. The surveillance intervals were then computed by a deterministic rule engine encoding guideline rules. We evaluated extraction performance on 100 procedures (215 pots), assessed surveillance recommendation performance on a same-site cohort (n=100), and performed external validation on a cohort from a second trust (n=100). A separate retrospective audit compared automated recommendations and observed routine scheduling against a clinician-derived reference based on full electronic health record review in 127 patients. Results Key extraction fields showed end-to-end accuracy (specimen type=0.995; location=0.981; diagnosis=0.981; excision completeness=0.949), with mean report-level pot comprehensiveness of 0.968 (SD 0.112). Overall surveillance recommendation accuracy was 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98) at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust (GSTT) and 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-0.97) at Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust (SWB) and showed strong class-level performance (no follow-up F 1 -score of 0.98 at GSTT and 0.97 at SWB; site check F 1 -score of 0.93 at GSTT and 0.91 at SWB; 3-year follow-up F 1 -score of 0.86 at GSTT and 0.80 at SWB; cancer alert F 1 -score of 1.00 at GSTT and 1.00 at SWB). The comparison to current clinical practice showed that the tool would improve guideline adherence primarily by reducing potential undersurveillance. Conclusions This hybrid approach using open-weight large language models for structured extraction and guideline-encoded rules for decision-making can generate accurate, lightweight, and auditable postpolypectomy surveillance recommendations. Such a tool has the potential to improve safety netting and guideline adherence in NHS colonoscopy workflows.

title: AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings.
abstract: Background Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. Objective This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. Methods This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Results Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets. Conclusions Imaging-based AI for predicting PSS and PSE has progressed rapidly, but important methodological and geographical gaps remain. Limited external validation, heterogeneous reporting, and the absence of African development and validation cohorts restrict confidence in the generalizability of existing models. Future research should prioritize the development of explainable imaging-based AI models using representative African neuroimaging datasets and their external validation in multicenter studies.

title: Metastasis Extraction From Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Clinical Notes Using Large Language Model-Based Classification: Retrospective Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Identification of metastasis status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a critical part of understanding disease prognosis, treatment courses, trial eligibility, and population-level cancer surveillance. However, metastasis status is inconsistently recorded in structured cancer registry fields, since manual abstraction of clinical notes is often an error-prone process. This challenge highlights an opportunity for leveraging large language models (LLMs) to conduct high-scale metastasis extraction from real-world clinical documentation. Objective We conducted a retrospective, multicohort comparative evaluation of 3 distinct LLMs for 2 independent classification tasks: overall metastasis presence at any site and brain/central nervous system (CNS) metastasis presence. We evaluated model performance on 2 independent NSCLC cohorts: one with registry labels and another with manual annotations. We further explored whether our methods could analyze clinical documentation and recover missing information in structured registry fields. Methods Patient cohorts were derived from the Winship Cancer Institute. Cohort 1 (n=579 patients; 24,887 notes across 69 note types; 2023-2025) used registry-linked metastasis fields as the reference standard. Cohort 2 (n=22 patients; 644 radiology notes; 2010-2021) was drawn from 2 completed randomized trials and used dual-annotated labels (Cohen κ: 0.93 overall metastasis; 0.88 CNS metastasis) as the reference standard. We fine-tuned the GatorTron-base encoder model for each independent binary classification task. We evaluated MedGemma-27B-text and Llama 3.1-70B using zero-shot prompting. A separate cohort of 675 patients with missing registry labels was used for an exploratory missingness-recovery analysis, validated against annotations of a random subsample. Our best-performing model was used to conduct further site-specific metastasis classification, based on available registry data. Results More than half (675/1260, 54%) of initially identified cohort 1 patients had missing or unknown registry metastasis labels. MedGemma demonstrated the best performance in overall metastasis classification (cohort 1: F 1 -score=0.80; cohort 2 patient-level: F 1 -score=1.0; cohort 2 note-level: F 1 -score=0.93). For brain/CNS metastasis, Llama3 performed best in both cohorts (cohort 1: F 1 -score=0.79; cohort 2 patient-level: F 1 -score=0.93; cohort 2 note-level: F 1 -score=0.86). The fine-tuned GatorTron model showed strong performance for classification of overall metastasis in cohort 1 (F 1 -score=0.72). Error analysis indicated that several model errors reflected incomplete registry labels, ambiguous clinical language, or missing documentation. In the exploratory recovery analysis, model predictions agreed with manual annotations at an accuracy of 0.90 and F 1 -score of 0.89. Additional site-specific metastasis classification by MedGemma demonstrated high performance for liver metastasis (F 1 -score=0.82) and bone metastasis (F 1 -score=0.79). Conclusions All models demonstrated relatively high performance. The zero-shot generative models were more robust to nuanced documentation and context-dependent brain/CNS metastasis extraction. The fine-tuned encoder model demonstrated strong classification performance but may have been limited by potential inaccuracies in the registry reference standards during model training. This study further demonstrated the potential of LLMs in recovering plausible structured labels from narrative text, complementing cancer registries for metastasis ascertainment.

title: Survival disparities in primary malignant spine tumors: a national analysis of academic and community hospital care.
abstract: Objective Primary malignant osseous tumors of the mobile spine are rare and require complex, multidisciplinary care. Treatment outcomes may differ between academic and community hospitals due to variations in resources, expertise, and infrastructure. This study evaluates demographics, care delivery patterns, and clinical outcomes, including both short- and long-term survival, for patients treated at academic versus community cancer programs using the National Cancer Database. Methods A retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database was performed. Nine hundred forty-three patients diagnosed with primary malignant osseous tumors of the mobile spine between 2004 and 2017 were identified. Patients were stratified by facility type: there were 601 patients treated at academic comprehensive cancer programs (ACADs) and 342 treated at comprehensive community cancer programs (CCCPs). Demographic, treatment, and clinical data were compared using descriptive statistics. Outcomes included inpatient length of stay, time to treatment, 30- and 90-day mortality, vital status at last contact, and overall survival. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model assessed factors associated with overall survival. Results Patients at ACADs were significantly younger and more likely to have private insurance. The size and histopathological composition of the tumors did not differ significantly between facility types. ACAD patients experienced significantly longer inpatient stays and longer time to radiation initiation among patients receiving radiation with documented start dates. Time to chemotherapy did not significantly differ (p = 0.91). Thirty- and 90-day mortality were comparable between facility types among eligible surgical cases. At last follow-up, a significantly greater proportion of ACAD patients were alive (50.2% vs 38.3%, p < 0.001), and the median time from diagnosis to last contact or death was longer at ACADs (40.8 vs 33.2 months, p = 0.001). In the primary multivariable Cox model, treatment at an academic facility was associated with improved overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0.766, 95% CI 0.627-0.937; p = 0.009). In a sensitivity model adjusting for histopathology rather than grade, this association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (CCCP vs ACAD, HR 1.19, p = 0.081). Conclusions Patients treated at academic centers had longer inpatient stays and longer time to radiation initiation, yet academic facility treatment was associated with improved overall survival in the primary multivariable model. After accounting for histopathological subtype in sensitivity analysis, the facility-type association was attenuated, suggesting survival differences reflect both tumor biology and system-level care pathways.

title: Spatial localization patterns in MRI-negative Cushing disease: a comparative pituitary heat map analysis.
abstract: Objective MRI-negative Cushing disease is challenging to treat due to difficulty with tumor localization and lower biochemical remission rates. Surgeons primarily rely on visual and tactile feedback to identify abnormal pituitary tissue. In this study, the authors analyzed intraoperative sketches of histology-confirmed corticotroph adenomas to compare the spatial distributions of MRI-positive and MRI-negative tumors. By characterizing these distribution patterns, the authors aimed to improve the localization and surgical targeting of MRI-negative pathology. Methods The authors retrospectively reviewed patients with Cushing disease who underwent microscopic transsphenoidal resection by the late Dr. Edward H. Oldfield at the authors' institution from December 2007 to March 2017. Patients were stratified into MRI-positive and MRI-negative cohorts. A standardized pituitary sketch visualizing both coronal and sagittal planes was used for postoperative documentation. For every patient, Dr. Oldfield annotated the anatomical location of the histologically confirmed corticotroph adenoma. Image acquisition, processing, and heat map-based spatial analysis were performed to assess cumulative tumor density. Spatial differences were evaluated with cluster-based correction for multiple comparisons. Surgical outcomes were then compared between the 2 cohorts. Results A total of 153 patients with Cushing disease and histologically confirmed pituitary corticotroph adenoma (133 MRI-positive and 20 MRI-negative adenomas) were analyzed. Baseline demographic and biochemical characteristics were similar across MRI status. Both cohorts demonstrated similar anatomical presentation, with over 50% of patients presenting with corticotroph adenomas in the anterior aspect of the pituitary gland. MRI-positive tumors were more likely to localize to the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary (p < 0.05). In contrast, MRI-negative adenomas showed no distinct area of increased prevalence. Postoperatively, the MRI-negative cohort had higher nadir cortisol levels (2.9 vs 1.5 μg/dl, p = 0.001) and increased reoperation rates (20% vs 3.8%, p = 0.027). Remission rates were lower in MRI-negative patients but not statistically significant (75.0% vs 91.0%, p = 0.050). Conclusions MRI-negative corticotroph adenomas were less frequently localized in the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary compared to MRI-positive tumors, with no distinct region of increased prevalence. These findings support a unique surgical strategy that leverages the anatomical distribution of histologically confirmed adenomas to guide gland exploration and resection of hidden tumors. While these observations may provide anatomical context for surgical exploration in radiographically occult disease, operative decision-making should remain guided by intraoperative findings and individual patient anatomy.

title: Quantitative MRI to assess baseline shunt flow in patients with hydrocephalus: a noninvasive tool to aid clinical decision-making.
abstract: Objective Hydrocephalus is a common yet serious condition, and ventricular shunts are used for lifesaving CSF diversion. Existing methods for shunt evaluation provide correlative/qualitative information, leading to commonplace clinical diagnostic challenges. The aim of this study was to determine accurate and noninvasive measures of volumetric CSF flow rates through ventricular shunts using the phase-contrast (PC) sequence in routine MRI for pediatric patients with hydrocephalus. Methods The authors conducted a prospective observational cohort study of patients with ventricular shunts who underwent a clinically indicated brain MRI and the adjunct PC-MRI shunt flow sequence at a single center between January 2023 and January 2024. At the study institution, PC-MRI has been integrated as a supplementary imaging technique to quantify shunt flow alongside fast protocol MRI for shunted patients. Clinical and imaging data were collected. Data distributions and paired changes in flow measurements over time were assessed using appropriate statistical tests. Results Overall, 207 patients (107 male, mean age 11.3 years [range 8 days-27 years]) who underwent PC-MRI were included; 98% had a VP shunt. The mean CSF flow rate was 9.9 ± 8 mL/hour (range 0.5-54 mL/hour). No significant differences were noted by age, sex, etiology of hydrocephalus, valve type, time interval since shunt placement, BMI, fronto-occipital horn ratio, and frontal horn or atrial width. Repeat PC-MRI was performed in 11 patients, and there was no significant difference in flow measurements between initial and follow-up images (p = 0.83) among these patients. PC-MRI identified alterations that accurately demonstrated failure in 3 patients and avoided unnecessary surgery in a fourth patient. Conclusions Addition of PC-MRI to routine imaging examinations in patients with ventricular shunts accurately and noninvasively measured CSF shunt flow. Flow rate data can provide supplementary information regarding shunt function and serve as a baseline for future comparison assessments. These findings suggest a role for routine acquisition of patient-specific baseline shunt flow measurement in shunted pediatric patients with hydrocephalus.

title: Mixed Pneumonia with Pulmonary Embolism and Multiple Pathogens Detected in Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid: A Case Report.
abstract: Severe community-acquired pneumonia may involve mixed pathogens and concurrent vascular complications. A 72-year-old man presented with fever, nonproductive cough, vomiting, hypoxemia, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and an elevated D-dimer concentration. Chest computed tomography showed left lower-lobe consolidation and pleural effusion. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography, obtained because of hypoxemia and suspected pulmonary embolism, showed a filling defect in a right upper-lobe pulmonary artery. The patient received antimicrobial therapy prior to bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Bronchoscopy was performed in the bronchopulmonary segment corresponding to the radiographic lesion, and approximately 10 mL of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) was recovered aseptically for microbiological and cytological testing. An aliquot of at least 3 mL was allocated to a multiplex pathogen-targeted sequencing assay, which detected Chlamydia psittaci, influenza A H3N2, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and additional conditionally pathogenic or commensal organisms. The three principal detections were interpreted in conjunction with the clinical presentation, imaging, inflammatory markers, BALF cytology, conventional testing, and treatment response. The patient improved during antimicrobial and anticoagulant treatment and was discharged on December 3, 2025. At the documented outpatient follow-up on December 17, rivaroxaban was continued for approximately one further month. This case highlights the adjunctive value and interpretive limitations of targeted sequencing in a treated patient. The serial imaging and invasive sampling reflected case-specific decisions and should not be interpreted as a routine protocol for pneumonia.

title: A Standardized Workflow for Multimodal Assessment of Right-to-Left Shunt-Related Ischemic Brain Injury.
abstract: Right-to-left shunt (RLS) has been associated with cryptogenic stroke, migraine, and other neurological conditions in which ischemic brain injury may be clinically relevant. In routine practice, however, assessment is often fragmented. Shunt presence may be documented, but shunt burden, provoked versus non-provoked patterns, anatomical complexity, and MRI-defined brain injury are not always integrated into a reproducible workflow. Here, we describe a standardized protocol for multimodal assessment of RLS-related ischemic brain injury in a clinically selected cohort. The workflow includes patient screening, exclusion of major vascular and systemic factors that could independently contribute to brain parenchymal injury, contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler ultrasound (c-TCD) confirmation and shunt grading, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) classification, transthoracic and/or transesophageal echocardiographic anatomical assessment, structured data extraction, and dataset cleaning. To improve reproducibility, the protocol also standardizes key coding steps, including shunt-grade harmonization, classification of RLS as simple or complex, and interpretation of D-dimer values reported below the assay threshold. Using this workflow, a harmonized analytic cohort of 60 RLS-positive patients was established. MRI identified 23 MRI-negative and 37 MRI-positive patients. Representative analyses showed that MRI-positive findings were more frequent in patients with greater shunt burden and more complex anatomical phenotypes. This protocol provides an operational model for incorporating c-TCD, MRI, echocardiography, and structured clinical parameters into the evaluation of MRI-defined ischemic brain injury in RLS-positive patients. It should be interpreted as a workflow for standardized multimodal phenotyping rather than as a standalone physiologic assessment of all clinically significant or hypoxemia-related RLS.

title: HeartFusion: A Cross-Modality Transformer for Accurate Cardiovascular Disease Diagnosis and Severity Assessment.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) requires diagnostic models that can integrate complementary electrophysiological and anatomical information while also representing ordered disease severity. HeartFusion was developed as a mathematically informed cross-modality Transformer framework combining electrocardiogram (ECG) and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Wavelet-derived ECG time-frequency representations were encoded with Cardioformer, MRI structure was encoded with TransUNet, and modality-specific embeddings were aligned in a shared latent space using cosine-similarity-based cross-modal attention. A transformer classifier performed diagnostic prediction, while an ordinal regression head modeled four ordered severity stages. Three controlled pseudo-paired benchmark cohorts were constructed from PTB-XL with ACDC (CVD-I), MIMIC-IV-ECG with CMRxRecon (CVD-II), and PTB-XL/MIMIC-IV-ECG with OCMR/Cardiac Atlas Project data (CVD-III). Source observations were partitioned before pseudo-pair construction to prevent cross-partition leakage, and five matched random seeds were used for evaluation. HeartFusion achieved diagnostic accuracies of 97.73%, 98.23%, and 98.02%, with AUC values of 98.12%, 98.76%, and 98.39% on CVD-I, CVD-II, and CVD-III, respectively. Severity staging achieved ordinal accuracies above 90%, with the best Cohen's kappa of 0.839 and MAE of 0.340. These findings support phenotype-level multimodal representation learning, while validation on genuinely patient-matched ECG-MRI cohorts remains necessary before clinical deployment.

title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

title: Clinical Application of Three-dimensional Laparoscopic Artery-first Pancreaticoduodenectomy in Treating Pancreatic Head Malignant Tumors.
abstract: Pancreaticoduodenectomy is a technically demanding procedure associated with substantial surgical risk. Conventional laparoscopic approaches have several limitations, including restricted visualization, which can make exposure of the superior mesenteric artery and identification of vessels and lymph nodes challenging. In patients with vascular adhesion or tumor invasion, surgical dissection is particularly difficult and may increase the risk of intraoperative vascular injury and hemorrhage. In addition, poor delineation of anatomical planes may result in incomplete tumor dissection, inadequate lymphadenectomy, and difficult mobilization of the pancreatic head and duodenum, potentially compromising surgical safety and oncological outcomes. To optimize the surgical workflow, this protocol describes a three-dimensional laparoscopic artery-first pancreaticoduodenectomy with the infracolic artery-first approach as the principal technical modification. By combining early arterial exposure and clear delineation of anatomical planes with the stereoscopic visualization of three-dimensional laparoscopy, this technique facilitates identification of vessel-tissue relationships, vascular control, lymphadenectomy, tumor dissection, and tissue mobilization. These features may help reduce inadvertent vascular injury and intraoperative blood loss while enabling complete tumor resection. The protocol provides a standardized surgical approach, particularly applicable to pancreatic head lesions adjacent to or involving major vessels, and is intended to improve the safety and reproducibility of laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy.

title: Structural Evaluation of Retinal and Choroidal Features in Eyes With Primary Microtropia.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the structural characteristics of the macula, optic nerve head, and choroid in eyes with primary microtropia using spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT). Methods This prospective case-control study included 50 pediatric patients with a diagnosis of primary microtropia. Each participant contributed data from both eyes. Eyes were categorized as microtropic, fellow, or healthy control. All patients underwent comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation, including SD-OCT imaging. Parameters assessed included central macular thickness, total macular volume, regional retinal thickness, peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thickness, subfoveal and regional choroidal thickness, and choroidal vascular index. Results No statistically significant differences were observed among microtropic, fellow, and control eyes in terms of central macular thickness, total macular volume, or peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thickness ( P > .05). Although microtropic eyes showed a mild trend toward increased parafoveal and perifoveal retinal thickness across all quadrants, this variation did not reach statistical significance. Similarly, subfoveal, nasal, and temporal choroidal thickness measurements, as well as choroidal vascularity index, luminal area, stromal area, and total choroidal area, were comparable across all groups. Conclusions Primary microtropia was not associated with measurable retinal or choroidal structural abnormalities on SD-OCT. Although reduced visual acuity was present, the lack of detectable anatomical changes warrants further investigation to determine whether functional impairment in microtropia occurs independently of structural alterations.

title: Evaluation of Macro- and Microstructural White Matter Changes in Hot Water Epilepsy.
abstract: Background and objectives Hot water epilepsy (HWE) is a form of reflex epilepsy and usually lacks definitive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features. Although white matter abnormalities have been extensively investigated in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy or generalized epilepsies, very few studies have examined quantitative changes in reflex epilepsy. This study aims to explore the white matter changes in HWE. The objective is to investigate the white matter micro- and macrostructural changes in patients with HWE using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) indices and three-dimensional structural-imaging-derived subcortical white matter volumes. Methods Eighty-eight subjects with HWE and 50 age- and sex-matched controls underwent high-resolution volumetric MRI and DTI. DTI and volumetric data were processed using tract-based spatial statistics and FreeSurfer, respectively. Between-group differences in DTI metrics and regional subcortical white matter volumes were assessed. Correlations between DTI metrics, white matter volumes, and epilepsy-specific clinical variables were also evaluated. Results Subjects with HWE showed significant alterations in DTI metrics indicative of impaired white matter integrity, including decreased fractional anisotropy and increased mean diffusivity, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity. These changes were evident both globally (whole-brain) and within specific supratentorial and infratentorial white matter tracts. Subcortical white matter volume loss was predominant in the thalamo-limbic, somatosensory, posterior cingulate, cuneus, and frontal regions. Positive correlations were observed between alterations in global fractional anisotropy and changes in macrostructural (subcortical) white matter volumes. Conclusion Subjects with HWE exhibited global and region-specific white matter alterations at both micro- and macrostructural levels. Somatosensory subcortical involvement may be associated with the stimulus sensitivity characteristic of this disorder. Involvement of temporal-limbic and default mode network regions is consistent with the clinical semiology, while brainstem changes concur with the reflex nature of the disease.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease misdiagnosed as angle closure: Demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, and visual outcomes.
abstract: Purpose To describe the clinical presentation, diagnostic delay, management, and visual outcomes of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) disease presenting initially as angle closure. Methods This retrospective study reviewed the medical records of patients diagnosed with VKH who initially presented with angle closure between January 2013 and December 2020. Clinical features, intraocular pressure (IOP), imaging, treatment modalities, and final visual outcomes were analyzed. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to identify factors influencing final BCVA (best corrected visual acuity). Results Among 768 VKH patients, 18 patients (36 eyes; 3.94%) presented with angle closure with a mean age of 44.4 years and a female preponderance (89%). Eighteen eyes had primary angle closure (PAC), and 18 eyes had secondary angle closure glaucoma (SACG) at presentation. The mean IOP at final follow-up decreased from 26.3 to 14 mmHg. Fundus evaluation was deferred in many due to media opacities, leading to delayed VKH diagnosis (median delay: 1 month to 7 years). Ancillary imaging revealed choroidal thickening and ciliochoroidal effusion in four eyes. Poorer presenting BCVA and delayed diagnosis (>1 month) were associated with worse final BCVA ( P = 0.011 and P = 0.0066, respectively) in univariate analysis, while presenting BCVA remained a statistically significant independent predictor of final visual outcome (p 0.039) in multivariate analysis. Conclusion VKH can uncommonly present as angle closure, often mimicking PAC or SACG. Early clinical suspicion, use of posterior segment imaging (optical coherence tomography, B-scan, ultrasound biomicroscopy), and prompt immunosuppressive therapy are essential for optimal management.

title: Dual-energy computed tomography pulmonary angiography for pulmonary embolism: a three-tier evidence framework to guide individualized low-iodine scanning.
abstract: Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is widely studied for pulmonary embolism (PE) evaluation, but heterogeneity in protocols, platforms, and study designs complicates its clinical positioning. This narrative review, with structured search elements adapted from the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020, synthesized evidence from PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (January 2016-June 2026); 28 studies were eligible (26 of 1,287 screened records and 2 identified through citation tracing). Evidence was organized into a three-tier framework (image quality, diagnostic performance, and clinical outcomes). Low-keV virtual monoenergetic imaging at 40-50 keV improves vascular attenuation and enables iodine load reduction to approximately 6 g in selected protocols. Pooled meta-analytic evidence shows no consistent diagnostic advantage of DECT over single-energy CT. The right ventricular/left ventricular diameter ratio remains the most stable prognostic indicator; DECT perfusion metrics have not surpassed it for mortality prediction. Iodine-map hypoperfusion in distal arteries is suspicious for, but not morphologically confirmed as, subsegmental PE; such findings carry a risk of overdiagnosis and warrant caution before anticoagulation. A body mass index- and estimated glomerular filtration rate-stratified protocol table with Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine 2011 evidence-level annotations is provided, and knowledge gaps in photon-counting CT, artificial intelligence, and cross-platform standardization are identified.

title: A defined multi-kingdom microbial consortium naturalizes the immune system of laboratory mice
abstract: Dirty mice experiments suggest that laboratory mice fail to model certain human immune responses due to their limited microbial exposure. The identity, nature, and number of microbes required to normalize the immune system are unknown. Through systematic screening, we uncovered unexpected cross-kingdom microbial interactions and identified four enteric microbes spanning viruses, fungi, and protists sufficient to reproduce key immunological features of pet store mice and adult humans. This consortium also altered cancer outcomes, shifting tumorigenesis toward the anatomical pattern of human familial adenomatous polyposis in ApcMin/+ mice and recapitulating the imperfect response of many patients to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy. Thus, surprisingly few microbes can profoundly reshape immune states and disease responses, providing a tractable approach to naturalize laboratory mouse immunity.

title: Childhood Trauma and Cortical Thickness in Bipolar Disorder with and without Psychosis: Effects by Diagnostic Group and Trauma Subtype
abstract: Abstract Background Bipolar disorder affects about 2-3% of the population and is associated with cortical abnormalities, with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP) reported to show more pronounced changes. It remains unclear whether childhood trauma is associated with cortical thickness differences across bipolar disorder subgroups, particularly in BDP. Methods Using the publicly available PARDIP (Psychosis and Affective Research Domains and Intermediate Phenotypes) data set, we examined whether childhood trauma was associated with cortical thickness differences among 120 individuals: 33 with bipolar disorder without psychosis (BD; 36% male), 38 with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP; 47% male), and 49 healthy controls (HC; 61% male). Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form (CTQ-SF), and T1-weighted MRI scans were processed with FreeSurfer to extract cortical thickness across the 68 Desikan-Killiany regions. Linear mixed effects models tested associations between CTQ subtype scores and cortical thickness and trauma-by-diagnosis interactions, with sensitivity analyses for medication class and illness duration following the ENIGMA guidelines. Results No cortical thickness difference survived correction for multiple testing. At the nominal level, BD showed reduced thickness relative to HC in cingulate, frontal and occipital regions, whereas BDP showed greater superior temporal thickness relative to BD. Sexual abuse was nominally associated with reduced temporal thickness. Exploratory trauma-by-diagnosis interactions suggested region- and subtype-specific patterns that did not survive correction. Medication class and illness duration showed no significant effects after FDR correction. Conclusions These exploratory findings suggest nominal, region-specific associations between childhood trauma subtypes and cortical thickness in bipolar disorder. However, no findings survived correction for multiple comparisons, so they should be read as preliminary and need replication in larger samples.

Conclusions These exploratory findings suggest nominal, region-specific associations between childhood trauma subtypes and cortical thickness in bipolar disorder. However, no findings survived correction for multiple comparisons, so they should be read as preliminary and need replication in larger samples.

title: Facilitating Valid Statistical Inference in Biomedical Image Synthesis
abstract: Generative AI for medical image synthesis is increasingly used to impute missing data and augment biomedical datasets. Yet despite achieving high computational similarity to their real-world counterparts, synthetic images remain uncommon in clinical research practice, in part because of concerns about their biological validity. Here, we evaluate whether synthetic images support reliable downstream statistical analysis and biological inference in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging. We find that associations between patient phenotypes and synthesized images can be severely attenuated. This is because synthesis methods typically omit clinically relevant covariates and therefore generate images that, although visually realistic, mask key biological differences. Furthermore, naive analyses treat synthesized images as if they were observed, ignoring the statistical uncertainty introduced by synthesis. Drawing on multiple imputation theory, we introduce Phenotype Aware Multiple Synthesis (PAMS), an analysis framework that requires no model retraining and instead adjusts synthesized output to recover valid biological estimates with appropriately calibrated uncertainty. Applied to MRI and mIF data, PAMS reduced estimation bias and restored nominal confidence interval coverage. Because it is compatible with existing synthesis pipelines, PAMS offers a practical and rigorous route to statistically and biologically valid use of synthesized images in biomedical imaging research.

title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease
abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder′s eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold, so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90—0.96): after this representation collapse happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder′s learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer′s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An easy task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11—26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

title: Small Bowel Volvulus Diagnosed and Treated Using Intraoperative Angiography in a Hybrid Operating Room: A Case Report.
abstract: Small bowel volvulus is a surgical emergency that may cause mesenteric ischemia; however, diagnosis may be difficult when bowel perfusion appears preserved. An 84-year-old man presented with recurrent postprandial abdominal pain and melena 6 months after a total pharyngolaryngectomy with a jejunal free flap reconstruction. Extensive endoscopic evaluations, including capsule endoscopy, revealed no bleeding source. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed the whirl sign at the root of the small-bowel mesentery with the narrowing of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), while bowel wall enhancement was preserved. Because the symptoms recurred after resuming oral intake, a hybrid surgery combined with angiography was planned for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The SMA angiography demonstrated significant stenosis without apparent bowel hypoperfusion. After the intra-arterial administration of alprostadil, distal mesenteric perfusion deteriorated on the angiography, and laparoscopic exploration revealed ischemic changes consistent with small bowel volvulus. Because laparoscopic reduction was difficult, an open reduction was performed. Repeat angiography confirmed the resolution of the SMA narrowing and the restoration of distal flow. The patient's symptoms resolved completely. The hybrid surgery enabled a functional assessment of mesenteric hemodynamics and immediate surgical treatment during a single procedure. It may be useful in selected patients with small bowel volvulus who have preserved bowel perfusion at rest but recurrent symptoms suggestive of intermittent mesenteric ischemia, and in whom the indication for surgical detorsion remains uncertain.

title: Pancreaticoduodenectomy after Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy with Preservation of Gastric Arterial Inflow: A Case Report.
abstract: Obesity is an established risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. As laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) has become increasingly prevalent, pancreatic surgeons may encounter malignancies in patients with a surgically altered gastric anatomy. Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) after an LSG is rare and requires meticulous preoperative planning to prevent ischemic and anastomotic complications. A 47-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI 59.1 kg/m2) underwent LSG. Twenty-three days later, obstructive jaundice led to the diagnosis of pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy and substantial weight reduction (BMI 34.9 kg/m2), subtotal stomach-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy with wedge resection of the superior mesenteric vein was performed. Preoperative CT confirmed the preservation and patency of both the left and right gastric arteries. The left gastric artery was preserved intraoperatively. Gastrojejunostomy was performed using a hand-sewn anastomosis between the greater curvature side of the sleeve stomach and the jejunum. The patient developed a grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula but was discharged with no ischemic complications. PD after an LSG is feasible, but careful vascular assessment, a preplanned reconstruction strategy, consideration of the patient's metabolic and nutritional status, and careful intraoperative assessment of the remnant stomach may enhance surgical safety.

title: L2GSSL: Label-Efficient Local-to-Global Self-Supervised Learning for Volumetric Healthcare Data
abstract: Healthcare institutions routinely accumulate high-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, but only a fraction can be annotated by experts. We present L2GSSL, a local-to-global self-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled volumes by decomposing pretraining into intra-slice and inter-slice representation spaces. A slice encoder learns view-invariant local features, and a global encoder aggregates the resulting tokens to model volumetric context. The stop-gradient isolates the local space from the global objective, while slice-wise execution and a three-phase schedule support training under constrained GPU memory. On LIDC-IDRI lung nodule malignancy classification, L2GSSL reaches $0.9229$ AUROC with only $10\%$ of the labels and $0.9377$ with $25\%$, exceeding the volume-level VICReg by $0.0229$ and $0.0294$, respectively. With all labels, the strongest supervised baseline exceeds L2GSSL by only $0.0044$ AUROC, consistent with self-supervised pretraining providing its greatest value when annotations are limited. Without adaptation to the external LNDb cohort, a model fine-tuned on $25\%$ of LIDC-IDRI obtains $0.8138$ AUROC and $0.7589$ AUPRC, improving over the strongest evaluated self-supervised baseline by $0.1130$ and $0.0954$. Experiments across data sources, thoracic and abdominal anatomy, downstream tasks, and two backbones examine healthcare-data variety, while lesion-slice masking shows that the predictions depend on lesion-bearing content.

title: A Decision-Aware Evaluation Protocol for Uncertainty in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical segmentation uncertainty is often evaluated with calibration error or pixel-level error-detection scores, but these metrics do not show whether uncertainty improves downstream review decisions. We propose a decision-aware evaluation protocol that separates uncertainty estimation from deferral policy and evaluates their combination under fixed review budgets: which pixels, regions, or images should be accepted, and which should be reviewed. The protocol reports fixed-budget error reduction, risk-coverage behaviour, region-level review proxies, structural failure modes, probability-derived baselines, and sensitivity to review assumptions. We instantiate it across retinal vessel, skin lesion, and polyp segmentation with multiple backbones and uncertainty estimators. Under matched inference budgets and canonical multi-layer MC Dropout, test-time augmentation (TTA) gives a stronger error-detection signal across matched MC--TTA comparisons, including architecture and dropout-placement checks. However, estimator rankings are not universal. For example, probability-derived scores remain competitive, deep ensembles can outperform TTA, learned deferral helps mainly when the base estimator is weak, and rankings can change with review unit, uncertainty target, correction assumptions, and cost model. Structural and second-observer analyses further show that boundary and thin-structure failures are partly tied to annotation ambiguity. These findings support evaluating uncertainty as an estimator-policy-review configuration, not as a standalone score map. title: Bridging the Markerless Tracking Validation Gap: Intraoperative X-ray Workflow Integration
abstract: Markerless intraoperative tracking of spinal anatomy via RGB-D sensors is a promising alternative to invasive bone-anchored fiducials, yet no existing clinical dataset provides independent subsurface ground truth for validating these methods. We address this gap with a clinically viable pipeline that derives per-vertebra 6-DoF pose from routine intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopy, co-registered to the RGB-D camera frame through a multimodal fiducial array detectable in both imaging modalities. Critically, the pipeline requires no additional radiation, instrumentation, or deviation from standard surgical workflows, relying solely on the fluoroscopic images already acquired during routine level checks. A calibrated transform chain links the vertebral pose recovered via multi-view 2D-3D CT-to-fluoroscopy registration to the RGB-D coordinate frame, enabling direct comparison of any markerless registration estimate against a subsurface reference. Ex vivo validation against optically tracked ovine vertebrae confirms end-to-end accuracy of 2.06 +- 0.29 mm and 3.35 +- 0.93 degrees, sufficient to serve as independent ground truth for methods with substantially larger errors. We demonstrate the pipeline's utility by evaluating two markerless registration strategies on clinical data spanning 11 vertebrae across 1,500 frames from three surgical sequences: the first such evaluation against an independent subsurface reference in a clinical setting. The proposed framework provides reusable infrastructure for benchmarking emerging markerless tracking methods on real surgical data.

title: Mixture of Multi-Sequence Feature Difference for Contrast-Enhanced MRI Synthesis
abstract: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) is crucial for accurately diagnosing and segmenting brain tumors. However, the acquisition of CE-MRI requires injecting contrast agents, which poses potential health risks and increases scan costs. Here, we propose a CE-MRI synthesis method from non-contrast sequences, reducing both risk and cost. Unlike existing methods that rely on channel-wise concatenation to fuse multi-sequence information for synthesis, we introduce a Mixture of Feature Difference (MoFD) module. The proposed module uses a dynamic weighting strategy to adaptively select and aggregate informative features from both individual source sequences and explicit differences among them. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms baselines in terms of image fidelity and perceptual quality on the UCSF-PDGM and UPenn-GBM datasets. Our method successfully reconstructs tumor regions and achieves segmentation performance comparable to that obtained with real CE-MRI. Our ablation studies show that although adversarial learning improves perceptual quality, a regression-based variant of our method achieves higher structural fidelity.
